text: They have not answered her, and she has never been paid.
If somebody had read clause seven, she would not be here today.

To wrap up: she has never asked for anything else, and she is not asking for it now.

The last speech is the only one where you are not allowed to bring anything new, and that is the whole difficulty of it. Everything you could possibly say has already been said, by you or by the other side, and the room has heard all of it. So the only things left to choose are the order and the weight. Which sentence goes first, and what is the room looking at when you stop. The thing I spend most of my time arguing about with people I train is the weakest point. Everybody wants to leave it alone and hope. Concede it in the first minute, before the other side gets anywhere near it. A point you concede yourself costs you almost nothing. The same point taken from you costs the room's trust in every other thing you have said, and you never get that back inside ninety seconds. And about nerves, because somebody always asks. Poise is a skill, not a temperament. I have never met anybody who was not nervous. The two things that make a person look poised are a plan short enough to read at a glance, and being willing to stop talking early. That is it. Nobody has ever complained that a closing argument was too short.

Between my first mock mediation and my tenth, my vocabulary did not change at all. I want to be honest about that, because everybody assumes it must have. I knew almost exactly the same words on the first day as I did at the end, and I was just as nervous in the tenth as I was in the first. Nobody stops being nervous. What changed was that I stopped abandoning sentences halfway through. That was it, and I only noticed because somebody in the group was counting. In the first session I started and dropped eleven sentences in four minutes. Eleven. By the tenth it was two, and the two were on purpose, because I had thought of something better. Nobody who watched me would have said I had learned more English. They would have said I sounded like somebody who knew what he was doing. So when people come to me now and say they need more vocabulary before they can do this, I tell them what I wish somebody had told me. Almost nobody in my group needed more words. What they needed was to finish the sentence they had already started. That is a habit, not a level, and habits change in weeks.
Let me open with the one thing nobody in this room disputes.
There are two points, and I will signpost the second one before I make it.
I will concede this myself: she should have written again in April.
I am not going to labour the point, so I will say it once.
